crude.label: Crude oil in storage (commercial)
crude.what: Crude oil held in US tanks and pipelines, not counting the emergency reserve.
crude.why: Rising stocks mean supply is outrunning demand, which tends to weigh on prices. Falling stocks mean the opposite.

spr.label: Strategic Petroleum Reserve
spr.what: The government's emergency crude stockpile, held in salt caverns on the Gulf Coast.
spr.why: Releases add supply in a crisis; refilling it adds demand. Its level is a policy choice, not a market signal.

prod.label: US crude oil production
prod.what: How much crude the US pumps each day. The US has been the world's largest producer for years.
prod.why: Shale drilling responds to prices within months, which is why high prices tend to bring more supply.

imports.label: Crude imports
imports.what: Crude the US buys from other countries.
imports.why: Shows how much the US relies on the world market, and which way the trade is moving.

exports.label: Crude exports
exports.what: Crude the US sells abroad (allowed since 2015).
exports.why: Links US prices to the world market: more exports pull US prices toward Brent.

refutil.label: Refinery utilization
refutil.what: How much of the country's refining capacity is running.
refutil.why: Refineries turn crude into gasoline and diesel. Near 95% means they are running flat out, so pump prices can rise even if crude does not.

gasstock.label: Gasoline in storage
gasstock.what: Finished gasoline and blending components held in storage.
gasstock.why: Low gasoline stocks in the driving season push pump prices up.

diststock.label: Diesel and heating oil in storage
diststock.what: Distillate fuel oil: diesel for trucks, trains and farms, and heating oil.
diststock.why: Diesel moves freight and farming costs, so tight stocks feed into prices across the economy.

demand.label: Total petroleum demand (product supplied)
demand.what: How much oil product the US consumed that week (a close stand-in for demand).
demand.why: The cleanest weekly read on whether people and businesses are using more or less fuel.

events.title: Gulf War shock
events.text: Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990. Oil roughly doubled in a few months, from about $20 to above $40 a barrel.

events.title: Asian crisis glut
events.text: Weak Asian demand and rising supply pushed oil to about $11 a barrel, among the lowest prices in decades once inflation is counted.

events.title: The 2008 peak
events.text: Oil peaked near $145 in July 2008, then fell by about three-quarters in six months as the financial crisis cut demand.

events.title: The shale price war
events.text: OPEC chose not to cut output while US shale boomed. Prices fell from over $100 in mid-2014 to under $30 by early 2016.

events.title: Prices below zero
events.text: Pandemic lockdowns emptied roads and airports, and storage filled. On April 20, 2020 the front-month WTI futures contract settled below zero for the first time.

events.title: Russia-Ukraine
events.text: After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, sanctions and fears for supply sent Brent above $125 in early March.

source: US Energy Information Administration (via FRED and EIA open data), Yahoo Finance (futures), US Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPI)
